column5: Benign scheduling or execution errors should be coded as SEF.

column7: ROS 1 topic, service, TCPROS, UDPROS, or XMLRPC traffic is transmitted in plaintext.
column8: The study directly analyzes plaintext communication, eavesdropping, or absent channel protection.

column7: The ROS Master or node endpoints can be discovered or reached from outside the intended local network because access restrictions are absent or inadequate.
column8: The study provides evidence of exposed ports, Internet scanning, remote reachability, or open interfaces.
column9: Do not code when communication is confined to the intended local network and external exposure is not demonstrated.
column10: Open ROS ports, an exposed Master, or Internet-scan results.

column7: Nodes are not authenticated when registering, publishing, subscribing, or providing services.
column8: The study demonstrates malicious node registration, service hijacking, node impersonation, or authentication bypass.
column9: Benign node-name, topic-name, or namespace mistakes belong to ICF.
column10: Service re-registration, node impersonation, or absence of certificate/challenge validation.

column7: Network-visible nodes can publish, subscribe, or invoke sensitive topics and services without authorization.
column8: The study demonstrates unauthorized publishing, subscribing, service invocation, message injection, or replay.
column9: Accidental topic wiring or type mismatches belong to ICF.
column10: Forged /cmd_vel messages, unauthorized service calls, or topic injection.

column7: The ROS 1 Parameter Server lacks adequate authentication or authorization, enabling unauthorized parameter reads or writes.
column8: An attacker directly reads, overwrites, or manipulates runtime parameters.
column9: Benign incorrect parameter values or parameter paths should be considered BSE or ICF, respectively.
column10: Unauthorized modification of thresholds, control gains, or configuration parameters.

column5: Master as a Single Point of Failure
column7: Failure or attack of the centralized ROS Master can disrupt name resolution, discovery, or system coordination.
column8: The study explicitly exploits or evaluates the centralized weakness of the ROS Master.
column9: Ordinary node startup failures, build failures, or a crash of one non-Master node do not belong here.
column10: Master crashes, SlowROS, or graph-resolution failure.

column5: Lack of Flow Control and QoS
column7: ROS 1 lacks adequate rate limiting, priority, queue control, or QoS guarantees, and this deficiency is exploited by malicious traffic.
column8: An attacker causes overload or denial of service through high-rate publishing, connection occupation, or selective message suppression.
column9: Benign callback blocking, queue configuration, or executor problems belong to SEF.
column10: Topic flooding, subscriber overload, or message loss.

column7: DDS-Security or SROS2 does not fully encrypt traffic, or handshake, policy, or metadata remains exposed.
column8: The study directly analyzes partial encryption, signing without encryption, or metadata leakage.
column9: Ordinary message-format or semantic errors do not belong here.
column10: Observed handshake metadata, permission information, or unencrypted payloads.

column7: Node- or topic-level permissions lack the granularity needed to protect individual messages or fields.
column8: An over-privileged node reads protected messages and relays them to an unsecured channel.
column9: Benign publisher/subscriber mismatches belong to ICF.
column10: Confused-deputy behavior or protected data relayed to an insecure topic.

column7: External cryptographic libraries or components on which ROS 2 security depends can be replaced, tampered with, or compromised through the supply chain, undermining security guarantees.
column8: The study explicitly analyzes compromise of a cryptographic dependency and its effect on session keys or encryption.
column9: Ordinary dependency declarations, builds, or installation errors belong to BDF.
column10: OpenSSL or cryptographic-library replacement and session-key leakage.

column7: Certificates, keys, governance files, or permission files lack adequate local integrity protection.
column8: An attacker modifies, replaces, or downgrades credentials or policies to impersonate an identity or escalate privileges.
column9: Non-malicious policy syntax or configuration errors should be coded as REL only when the study analyzes them as reliability faults.
column10: Permission-file modification, certificate replacement, or privilege escalation.

column7: Messages are not reliably bound to a specific legitimate publisher, allowing an authorized node to impersonate another publisher on a shared topic.
column8: The study demonstrates source forgery or publisher impersonation on a shared topic.
column9: Benign frame-name, topic-name, or namespace mistakes belong to ICF.
column10: A forged publisher on /tf or another shared topic.

column7: Authenticated nodes can generate harmful traffic because rate limiting, throttling, or backpressure is absent or inadequate.
column8: An authenticated publisher or service client causes denial of service through flooding.
column9: Benign application-level callback overload or execution delay belongs to SEF.
column10: Authenticated topic flooding or service-call flooding.

column7: CPU, memory, process, or container resources are insufficiently isolated between nodes, allowing one malicious or faulty node to degrade the entire system.
column8: The study treats missing resource isolation as the primary security weakness and evaluates cross-node effects.
column9: A generic memory leak belongs to GPE; ordinary scheduling contention belongs to SEF.
column10: CPU or memory monopolization and cascading service disruption.

column7: The root cause lies in package manifests, dependency declarations, build/install/export scripts, workspaces, or deployment packaging.
column8: Missing or spurious dependencies, incorrect rosdep keys, malformed package.xml files, or incorrect CMake/ament/catkin/colcon rules.
column9: Source-code syntax or logic errors belong to GPE; launch wiring or path binding belongs to ICF.
column10: Build logs, manifests, dependency differences, or installation/export failures.

column7: The root cause lies in ROS callbacks, queues, executors, spin calls, callback groups, priorities, deadlines, or real-time scheduling.
column8: Callback starvation, queue overflow, missed deadlines, executor contention, or incorrect spin/callback-group configuration.
column9: Name, type, or QoS compatibility problems belong to ICF; generic locking or data-race defects belong to GPE.
column10: Timing traces, executor configuration, queue behavior, callback latency, or deadlock evidence.

column7: The root cause is a language-level or algorithmic implementation error not specific to ROS interfaces, executors, or domain semantics.
column8: Out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, null dereference, unhandled exceptions, missing input validation, generic races/deadlocks, or algorithmic logic errors.
column9: ROS executor or callback-group errors belong to SEF; interface wiring belongs to ICF; physical or domain-semantic errors belong to BSE.
column10: Crash stacks, sanitizer reports, fuzzing triggers, or source-code locations.

column7: The root cause lies in relationships, interface contracts, or configuration bindings among ROS entities, including names, types, namespaces, remaps, endpoints, QoS, and launch wiring.
column8: Incorrect topic/service/action names or types, missing endpoints, incorrect namespaces/remaps, QoS incompatibility, or launch-path/wiring errors.
column9: Correctly delivered data with incorrect physical meaning belongs to BSE; callback/queue-induced loss belongs to SEF; malicious unauthorized communication belongs to VUL.
column10: Dangling publishers/subscribers, interface mismatches, or configuration/wiring evidence.

column7: The root cause lies in robot models, transform values or conventions, physical units, parameter meaning, task logic, domain constraints, or explicit behavioral properties.
column8: Unit confusion, incorrect TF values or conventions, invalid URDF/SDF mass, inertia, or joint limits, invalid control parameters, or violated properties/invariants.
column9: Observed incorrect behavior alone is insufficient; incorrect interface relationships belong to ICF; generic code logic errors belong to GPE.
column10: Comparison of expected semantics or constraints with actual values, models, or execution traces.

Data, messages, services, or configurations are modified, forged, injected, replayed, or reconfigured without authorization.
Flooding, CPU or memory exhaustion, Master/node overload, or denial of service.
The system continues to run but behaves incorrectly, inconsistently, unsafely, or with degraded functionality.
Build, deployment, or startup failure; node or system crash, freeze, deadlock, or inability to operate.
